googles-definition.description: Three Google authors define context engineering as “the practice of providing AI agents with rich, structured information about your codebase, architecture, conventions, and intent”, and list six kinds of context: instructions, knowledge, memory, examples, tools and guardrails. It is a practitioner whitepaper, not a study: it frames the term and does not test the parallel to requirements [1].

osmani-new-sdlc.title: Osmani, Saboo, Kartakis (Google), The New SDLC With Vibe Coding: From ad-hoc prompting to Agentic Engineering

the-definition.description: Anthropic defines context engineering as curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference, guided by "the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens" that maximize the chance of the desired outcome [1].

anthropic-effective-context-engineering.title: Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents

input-quality-tracks-output-quality.description: in a randomized experiment with 30 novices, training in requirement-oriented prompting beat conventional prompt-engineering training (20% against 1% gains), and the authors report input-requirement quality correlates with output quality. It is a small trip-advisor chatbot study, not coding agents [1].

ma-requirement-driven-llm-use.title: Ma, Peng, Yang, Shen, Koedinger, Wu, What Should We Engineer in Prompts? Training Humans in Requirement-Driven LLM Use

a-proposal-not-a-finding.description: researchers draw the parallel explicitly, but no source measured it; the sentence that both disciplines share a job is an inference [1].

chen-promptware-engineering.title: Chen, Wang, Sun, Liu, Zhang, Liu, Promptware Engineering: Software Engineering for Prompt-Enabled Systems

where-the-parallel-stops.description: a requirements document gains from completeness while a context window is a finite budget that can lose from it, and context changes during a run instead of being signed off once [1].

anthropic-effective-context-engineering.title: Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents

the-definition.title: The definition
the-definition.script: Here is how three Google engineers define context engineering, in their words: the practice of providing AI agents with rich, structured information about your codebase, architecture, conventions, and intent. That was written for software, but the logic is the same. Let me translate that from engineering into the workshop. The codebase is the materials you already have. The architecture is how the parts fit together. The conventions are the house rules. And the intent is the goal. Materials, how it fits, house rules, the goal: that is what a good requirement has always said. So what you add to the context window decides whether the agent has the precision and accuracy to work towards, and that is why we call it requirements engineering for agents.

same-four-outcomes.title: Same four outcomes
same-four-outcomes.script: Remember the dartboard with its four outcomes? It is the same dartboard, with the same four outcomes, but a different object. Your requirement document is now a context window, and it can land precise, accurate, both or neither.
